analysis.one_liner: Opens federal lands, offshore waters, and energy exports to oil, gas, and coal while stripping EPA climate authority.
analysis.headline: S. 2170, a sweeping bill to expand oil, gas, and coal development on federal land and end export limits, died in the Senate Energy Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote in the 113th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have lifted restrictions on exporting crude oil, natural gas, and coal; approved the Keystone XL pipeline by declaring no presidential permit needed; opened the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, and offshore waters to drilling; let states take over energy development on federal land free of federal environmental review; and declared that federal environmental laws do not authorize regulating climate change, voiding EPA greenhouse gas rules. It also blocked many courts challenges by capping injunctions at 60 days and barring attorney fee awards to groups whose lawsuits stop energy projects. It never received any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, oil and gas producers would have gained the right to export crude without federal restrictions, drill in the Arctic Refuge and offshore, and get drilling permits automatically approved after 60 days of inaction. Coal companies and export terminals would have faced environmental review limited to domestic impacts only. Pipeline developers would have gotten Keystone XL approved outright. Refineries would have gotten streamlined permits and relief from the renewable fuel mandate.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals presidential authority to restrict exports of oil, petroleum products, natural gas, and coal, and repeals statutory limits on crude oil exports, directing Commerce to grant crude export licenses by default [S2].

Approves TransCanada's Keystone XL pipeline by statute, declaring no presidential permit required and that the January 2014 environmental impact statement satisfies all National Environmental Policy Act requirements [S3].

Repeals the prohibition on oil and gas leasing in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, mandates annual lease sales in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska through 2023, and directs commercial oil shale lease sales in Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming [S2, S3].

Lets states elect to take over energy development on all available federal land within their borders, with certified state programs deemed to satisfy the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act, and exempt from federal judicial review [S3].

Declares that the Clean Air Act and four other major environmental laws neither authorize nor require regulation of climate change, redefines 'air pollutant' to exclude carbon dioxide, methane, and other greenhouse gases, and voids proposed EPA carbon pollution rules [S2].

Creates a Debt Freedom Fund to pay down the national debt and includes tribal provisions allowing the Navajo Nation to execute 99-year leases and mineral leases under approved tribal regulations without Interior Department approval [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Communities near new drilling, coal terminals, and pipelines would bear the local environmental effects, with injunctions against projects limited to 60 days and no attorney fees for groups whose lawsuits stop energy projects. The public would bear the climate consequences of the bill voiding EPA greenhouse gas regulation. Federal taxpayers would lease Arctic Refuge, offshore, and oil shale acreage, with revenue routed to a debt fund. Ethanol and renewable fuel producers would lose the federal mandate as it is phased out.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, near affected land and climate

drawbacks.text: The bill declares greenhouse gases outside the scope of the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, and the Solid Waste Disposal Act, eliminating the federal government's existing statutory basis for limiting carbon pollution [S2, S3].

It treats a 1987 environmental review of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as satisfying current law, requires analysis of only a leasing alternative (no nonleasing option), and limits the Secretary's authority to close coastal plain lands, leaving the refuge's future largely to lease terms written in 2014 [S3].

State energy programs on federal land would be exempt from federal judicial review and the Administrative Procedure Act, and drill permits would be deemed approved if the government misses a 60-day deadline, sharply reducing public recourse [S3].

It bars attorney fee awards to any organization whose litigation prevents or reduces energy production, and limits injunctions halting covered energy projects to 60 days, raising the cost of challenging federal energy decisions in court [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's promised benefits, chiefly jobs and growth from expanded energy production and exports, came bundled with a wholesale rollback of the legal framework protecting air, climate, and public land, including provisions exempting some state-run programs from any federal court oversight. Whatever benefit from smoother permitting and exports would have been purchased by removing climate authority from federal law and opening the Arctic Refuge to leasing. The bill offered little to offset those losses for the people who live near the development or breathe the emissions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never held a hearing or markup, and the 113th Congress ended with the bill dead.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced S. 2170 in the Senate on March 27, 2014, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S1, S5].
The committee took no further action; the bill's complete action history ends with the referral, with no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever scheduled [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, both sponsors being Republicans, in a Senate where Democrats held the majority and controlled the committee [S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing environmental safeguards, EPA greenhouse gas authority, and the Arctic Refuge leasing ban stayed in place because the bill never advanced, while the oil, gas, and coal interests it was written for gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept its environmental safeguards

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and its single cosponsor were Republicans, and the bill died in the Senate's Democratic-led Energy Committee without any hearing or vote.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed crude export restrictions, opened the Arctic Refuge, offshore waters, the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, and oil shale to drilling, auto-approved permits after 60 days, and let states take over federal-land development without federal judicial review. Its gains came largely from public land and relaxed environmental constraints, costs borne by the surrounding public.

industries.industry: Coal producers and export terminal operators
industries.note: Export authority would have been freed of presidential restriction, and environmental review for terminals and coal transport would have been limited to domestic impacts only, ignoring the effects of burning the coal overseas.

Cross-border pipelines would have gotten 120-day approvals with no presidential permit and no NEPA review, and Keystone XL would have been approved outright with judicial review confined to the D.C. Circuit.

The bill capped injunctions against energy projects at 60 days, barred attorney fee awards to groups whose suits reduce energy production, and exempted state-certified programs from federal judicial review, making legal challenges to energy development much harder.

Refineries would have gained streamlined permitting deadlines and relief from renewable fuel blending mandates, but repealing the crude oil export ban could have raised their domestic crude supply costs.
The bill phased out the Renewable Fuel Standard, removing the federal mandate that creates demand for ethanol and biodiesel.
